# Visualization using `ggplot2`

A very flexible approach to graphing in R uses the `ggplot2` package (take a look at the [overview](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2.html) on the package website).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
```
:::


::: callout-note
Why `gg`? GG stands for "grammar of graphics", as discussed by @ggplotbook. Loading `tidyverse` also gives you `ggplot2`.
:::

Let's work through an example first, using some data we have on weight and flipper length of 3 different species of penguins.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# install.packages("palmerpenguins")
library(palmerpenguins)
data(penguins)

penguins |> 
  select(species, body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 344 × 3
   species body_mass_g flipper_length_mm
   <fct>         <int>             <int>
 1 Adelie         3750               181
 2 Adelie         3800               186
 3 Adelie         3250               195
 4 Adelie           NA                NA
 5 Adelie         3450               193
 6 Adelie         3650               190
 7 Adelie         3625               181
 8 Adelie         4675               195
 9 Adelie         3475               193
10 Adelie         4250               190
# ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::
:::


Suppose we want to make a scatter plot with flipper length on the x-axis, and body mass on the y-axis. We set this information up in the `ggplot()` function like this:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(aes(x = ..., y = ...), 
       data = ...)
```
:::


and then add (with `+`) `geom_point()` to say we want to show the data with points. Note the warning which points out that data for 2 animals were missing and were not included in the plot.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_point()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](visualization_files/figure-html/scatter-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


We cannot see which animal is which species yet, but if we wanted to make each species a different color, we can add a color option:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, 
           color = species), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_point()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](visualization_files/figure-html/scattercolor-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Adding a few other options, we have a plot that could be used later in a publication or presentation.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, 
           color = species, shape = species), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("flipper length (mm)") + 
  ylab("body mass (g)") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(NULL),
         shape = guide_legend(NULL)) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", 
        legend.position.inside = c(0.15, 0.9))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![publication-ready figure](visualization_files/figure-html/penguinspublication-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::


Let's see how to make a boxplot.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g,
           color = species), 
       data = penguins) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("body mass (g)") +
  guides(color = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](visualization_files/figure-html/penguin boxplot-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Now let's try to make a boxplot for the primary outcome in our RCT, by treatment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
set.seed(20261019)
n <- 60
dat <- tibble(study_id = 1:(2 * n),
              first = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              last = sample(LETTERS, 2 * n, replace = TRUE),
              inclusion_over17 = 1,
              inclusion2 = 1, inclusion3 = 1, inclusion4 = 1,
              exclusion1 = 0, exclusion2 = 0,
              screened = 1,
              informed_consent = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              endpoints =  rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.9),
              age_today = floor(runif(2 * n, 25, 45)),
              gender = rbinom(2 * n, 2, 0.250),
              video_games = rbinom(2 * n, 4, 0.2),
              randomization_group = rep(0:1, n)) |> 
  mutate(reverse_digit = rnorm(2 * n, 3 + 2 * randomization_group, 1.5),
         reverse_digit = round(reverse_digit),
         cold_pressor = rnorm(2 * n, 60 - 10 * randomization_group, 20),
         cold_pressor = round(cold_pressor),
         video_challenge = rbinom(2 * n, 1, 0.2 + 0.3 * randomization_group)) |> 
  mutate(across(age_today:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(informed_consent == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  mutate(across(reverse_digit:video_challenge, ~ ifelse(endpoints == 1, .x, NA))) |> 
  select(-endpoints) 

sm <- dat |> 
  select(-(inclusion_over17:screened)) |> 
  rename(id = study_id,
         trt = randomization_group,
         age = age_today) |> 
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, 0:2, c("F", "M", "O")),
         trt = factor(trt, 0:1, c("control", "intervention")),
         video_games = factor(video_games, 0:3, 
                              c("<30 minutes per day", "30-60", "60-120", "120+"))) |> 
  filter(!is.na(trt), !is.na(reverse_digit))
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
sm |> 
  ggplot(aes(trt, reverse_digit)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("reverse digit span")
```

![](visualization_files/figure-html/plot-1.png){width=672}

In smaller studies, it's helpful to plot the observations as well as the summary boxplot. One good option for this is with a [beeswarm](https://r-graph-gallery.com/package/ggbeeswarm.html) plot, or by using [`geom_jitter`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_jitter.html). If there's not too much overlap in the outcome values between participants, `geom_point` might also work.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# install.packages("ggbeeswarm")
library(ggbeeswarm)

sm |> 
  ggplot(aes(trt, reverse_digit)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.2) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, outliers = FALSE) +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("reverse digit span") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:8, 
                     minor_breaks = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](visualization_files/figure-html/plotbeeswarm-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sm |> 
  ggplot(aes(trt, reverse_digit)) +
  geom_beeswarm() +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, outliers = FALSE) +
  xlab(NULL) + ylab("reverse digit span") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:8, 
                     minor_breaks = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](visualization_files/figure-html/plotbeeswarm-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


To save the graph, try the `ggsave()` function. It will save the most recent graph by default.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggsave("primary_beeswarm.jpg")
```
:::


When you need to combine graphs, [`patchwork`](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com) is great.  
  

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# install.packages("patchwork")

library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggplot(mtcars) + 
  geom_point(aes(mpg, disp))
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars) + 
  geom_boxplot(aes(gear, disp, group = gear))

p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](visualization_files/figure-html/patchwork-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::
